title: Agent report
description: What an agent hands back when it finishes one issue: a JSON file the orchestrator queries field by field, plus a path and at most two lines in chat. The orchestrator reads what it needs when it needs it instead of paying for a document on every later turn of the session. Validate with scripts/report_schema.py.
x-honesty-compatibility: What each contract declares about the contract IMMEDIATELY BELOW IT, and the only thing that lets a copy of this validator answer about a report older than itself (#416). `additive` means every document valid under the predecessor is valid under this version -- no enum member removed, no key newly required, no pattern tightened -- so an older report is a document this contract already covers. `breaking` and `unknown` and an absent entry all refuse, and they refuse for the same reason: the natural failure of a bump that forgot to declare is silence, and silence has to land on the side that over-refuses rather than the side that vouches for a contract nobody holds. A validator walks the chain from its own number down and stops at the first step that is not `additive`, so two steps back needs two declarations -- one claim about the last bump cannot carry a document from two contracts ago. It stops above 1 whatever is declared, because 1 is not a contract. THIS IS DECLARED, NEVER DERIVED: deciding subset by comparing two schema documents would need both, and a copy of this validator has exactly one -- the older schema is absent, not unread. The author records the relation at the bump, the one moment anybody holds both. WHAT IT COSTS: the declaration is stripped from the contract fingerprint, for the same reason x-schema-version is -- it is a claim about how contracts relate, not a constraint a document satisfies, and inside the fingerprint the comparison would be circular. So a declaration that is simply WRONG moves no hash and nothing here catches it; what a test can hold is that every recorded contract has one at all. GENERALISED FROM ONE INSTANCE, said plainly: 5 is the only additive bump this schema has ever had. 3 and 4 were both breaking in both directions, and 2 is `unknown` rather than `breaking` because the contract below it was never recorded. What is inferred from that instance is the shape of the question; what is NOT inferred is that additive bumps are common, or that a future one will be as easy to be sure about as adding two enum members and one optional key was.
x-honesty-versioning: The contract number this document implements, and the only place it is written down. A report carries the number it was written against in schema_version, and a copy of this validator compares the two. It is NOT in x-enforced, on purpose: everything in that list is something a report is refused over, and a version this copy does not hold is not a refusal. It is the third state -- unvalidatable by this copy -- and folding it into either of the other two recreates #212 one layer down, where an old copy announced a correct report as broken and nothing distinguished that from a malformed one. WHEN THE NUMBER MOVES: on any change to what a validator accepts or refuses, never on prose. That is deliberately not semver's answer. Because additionalProperties is false and no-unknown-keys is enforced, even adding an OPTIONAL key is breaking in one direction -- an older copy refuses a report the new contract permits, which is exactly the 0.3.0-refuses-docs case that filed #221 -- so the useful line is not major-versus-minor but enforcing-versus-annotation. scripts/report_schema.py takes a fingerprint of this document with the free prose stripped -- description, title, examples, the x-honesty narratives and x-convention -- and tests/test_agent_report_schema.py fails when the enforcing content moves without the number, and fails louder when the number moves to a value nothing recorded. x-enforced and x-enforced-on-disk are deliberately INSIDE the fingerprint although nothing reads them: they are this document's own statement of what a validator refuses, paired one-to-one with a mutation table, so a change there is nearly always a contract change and an unnecessary bump is cheaper than a missed one. What the fingerprint cannot see: the cross-field rules are Python in report_schema.py -- _RULES for the ones scoped to a single node, and functions called directly from validate() for the ones that span the whole report, such as the below-bar checks added in #411 -- so a rule that starts refusing something new without any keyword moving here changes the contract and leaves the hash untouched. VERSION 1 IS NOT A CONTRACT: it is the value every report written before anyone counted carries. Measured 2026-08-16, 57 of the 71 reports on disk say 1 and 14 name no version at all, written against at least three mutually incompatible schemas. None of them can be dated retroactively and back-stamping them would manufacture a claim, so 1 is left meaning before-anyone-counted and 2 is the first value that carries information.
x-honesty-on-disk: x-enforced-on-disk is the one place this validator leaves the report and touches the filesystem: it opens the pr_body payload, parses it, and checks the shape the forge needs -- and, since #274, one thing about the payload's CONTENT rather than its shape: whether the body binds a closing keyword to each issue pr_body.closes says merging it closes. Since #411 there is a second content check, built the same way: whether the body carries the pr_anchor each below-bar item says it was recorded at. Both are deliberately absence detectors rather than readers -- neither decides what a forge would close or whether a paragraph really explains a finding; the reasoning is under pr_body.closes and under adjacent.pr_anchor, and the limits they leave behind are named in x-convention. That is a deliberate exception to shape-only, because pr_body.state of 'written' is the report's one claim about a file the NEXT step consumes, and a body the forge rejects is discovered after the agent's session has ended. It is a separate list, run by a separate function, so nothing here can be mistaken for the shape pass: validate() never reads a file, and the command line says when it skipped the payload rather than staying quiet about it. Which file it opens is not the report's to choose: pr_body.path is resolved against the report's own directory and anything landing outside it is refused without being opened, and so is a path the containment question cannot be answered for at all -- there is no arrangement of this field that makes this validator read a file elsewhere on the machine.
x-honesty: This schema checks SHAPE, never TRUTH. A structured summary is easier to accept without reading than a paragraph is, and that is the trade being made here: a refused disposition renders identically whether the refusal was argued or lazy. Two lists below say which is which. x-enforced is what scripts/report_schema.py actually refuses a report over, and every name in it is paired with a mutation in tests/test_agent_report_schema.py that proves the refusal happens. x-convention is the rest -- real parts of the contract, checked by nobody, and listed here so the next person meets the limit at the same moment they meet the schema.
x-convention: that a survey marked checked was in fact checked -- nothing here can see whether a reviewer ever spawned
that a refusal's reason argues the point rather than restating the finding
that files matches what the commit actually touched
that every claim needing a grade appears in claims, and that the grades are honest
that summary is two lines rather than a document moved one field to the left
that summary and split_cost are non-empty at all -- both are required keys of type string, and an empty string satisfies that
that pushed is false, which the contract requires and this validator does not
that the agent writes a report at all -- an agent that ignores this document produces nothing for any assertion to see

that a below-bar item's pr_anchor being present in the body means the body actually records the finding -- containment is an absence detector and cannot read prose for substance, so an anchor pasted alone would pass; the length floor makes that cost a phrase rather than making it impossible

that a below-bar item recorded in the STATE ENTRY rather than the pull request is checked at all -- the manager's third receipt admits both, and the state entry is written by the maintainer after the agent's session has ended, so nothing here can see it. An agent's own receipt is the pull request body, which is why that is the one this validator requires

that a closing reference this validator did find is one the forge will honour -- pr_body.closes is checked by an absence detector, so a finding is strong and a pass is weak, and gh-pr-create remains the only thing here that reads a body the way a forge does

schema_version.description: The contract this report was written against -- x-schema-version of the schema the agent read. Typed and required, and deliberately NOT constrained to a value: a const here forbade recording a version at all, which is how the field sat at 1 across three incompatible schemas. Whether the number matches the copy doing the validating is not a shape question and is not decided here; scripts/report_schema.py decides it separately, in three states, so a report from another contract reads as unvalidatable rather than as malformed.

head.description: The commit the agent stopped on.

pushed.description: The contract says an agent never pushes. Recorded rather than assumed, so a run that was pushed is visible instead of silent.

summary.description: At most two lines. The whole of what the orchestrator reads before deciding push / review / bounce.

files.description: One entry per file the commit touches, one line each.

docs.description: One entry per path in the repo's docs_targets. The changelog half of the docs duty is gated on every pull request; this half is not, and a gate was measured on the plugin's own repository, against its last thirty merged pull requests, rather than assumed -- one repository's history, named as such rather than presented as a fact about the repo being worked in. The trigger the changelog gate already computes fires on 27 of 30 and is right about 6, and the narrowest rule worth testing (a new file under a product path) fires on none of the thirty at all. A rule wrong two times in three earns a blanket override label in a week, and one that never fires cannot be told from one that is broken. So the duty is observed here instead of enforced there, and this survey is the only record that it happened. state checked with no items means the config named no targets; not-checked means nobody opened them; the key being absent is refused outright, because that is the state this field exists to make unspellable.

claims.description: Claims the run could not observe on the machine it ran on -- platform legs above all. Not every sentence in the report: the set that needs a grade. A run that never assessed them says state not-checked and why, which is different from having none.

blocked.description: Steps that could not be taken -- a permission prompt on a git step, an unspawnable agent, a decision that is not the agent's to make. A permission block is reported, never routed around.

note_path.description: Absolute path to the long half, when one was written. Lives outside every worktree so it can never enter a diff.

split_cost.description: One line: roughly how much went to the note versus the report, and whether anything had to be left out of both. Without it the split is a guess that got adopted.

survey.description: Every list in this report is a survey, because an empty array cannot say whether anyone looked. checked with no items means looked and found nothing. not-checked means nobody looked, and must say why.

review_survey.description: A survey whose items come back from somebody else, so it carries a fourth state the other surveys cannot use. A docs sweep has no second party to go quiet; a spawn does. returned-nothing is a spawn that executed, consumed its budget and handed back an empty final message: the review happened and its conclusions are lost. That is not checked -- which would render a real review as a clean one, the whole of #200 -- and it is not not-checked, which claims nobody looked and understates what is missing. It carries a reason naming which spawn went quiet and what was lost, and unlike not-checked it MAY carry items, because whatever the caller re-derived from its own transcript belongs here with disposition open rather than nowhere. It dominates: one spawn going quiet makes checked unavailable however well the other one answered.

scope.description: Where it applies -- a platform, a Python version, a shell.

grade.description: observed: run here. reasoned: argued from the code, worth having, still not run. unobserved: named and not established.

action.description: What became of a defect nobody filed. The filing bar defines three receipts and this field encoded two until #411, so a lane that correctly decided the finding was below the bar and belonged in the pull request body had to label it `report-for-filing` and disclaim it in the free text underneath -- the label saying file this and the prose saying do not file this, in the same object. The maintainer read the label first and nearly filed it. `below-bar` is a phrase with no verb and no tense on purpose: `filed` was removed in #254 because past tense reads as an act the agent performed, and `report-for-filing` misreads here because an imperative reads as an act the reader should perform. Both failures are a verb being attributed to somebody; a statement of where the finding sits relative to the intake bar has no verb to attribute. It is the value for a real finding with no reachable caller -- a docstring wider than its code, a comment left by a fix, a receipt that overstates -- and it is not a way to be quiet about one: it carries `pr_anchor` and the on-disk pass checks the body actually says it.

pr_anchor.description: Required when the action is `below-bar`, and refused as a receipt when the pull request body does not carry it. A verbatim fragment of the body where this item is recorded -- write the line first, then quote enough of it here to find it again. Compared after whitespace is collapsed, so wrapping the body is free, with case folded, because the first report written against this check quoted a sentence its own body carried inside bold at the head of a bullet and a case-sensitive containment refused a receipt that was plainly there, and after HTML comments are removed, because a receipt nobody can read is not one; code spans are deliberately NOT stripped, unlike the closing-keyword check, since a reader sees a backticked sentence and a forge does not see a backticked keyword. Its standing is exactly the `closes` check's: an absence detector, so a finding is strong and a pass is weak. A body carrying the anchor and nothing else would pass, and nothing here can read prose for substance -- what the check buys is that a below-bar item can no longer be a silent drop wearing a decision's clothes. The length floor is the same admission: an anchor short enough to occur incidentally proves nothing, so it has to cost a phrase.

docs_target.description: One path from docs_targets, and what happened to it. updated needs no why -- the diff is the why. The other two do: 'no change needed' with no reason is the sentence a run that never opened the file also writes, and an unread target is a gap somebody can act on rather than the absence of a finding.

state.description: updated: this diff changed it. no-change-needed: you opened it and it is still true. not-read: you did not open it.

why.description: Required for no-change-needed (what you read it against) and for not-read (why not). The whole value of this survey is in this field.

tests.description: One object rather than two, so a run with a green and no red is a stated state instead of a missing key.

state.description: not-applicable is the honest answer for a prose-only change; not-run is the answer when a test should have been watched failing and was not.

mechanism.description: What actually ran, named exactly -- the subagent type and the brief it was pointed at -- or that nothing did, or that it ran and came back empty. A review that did not execute must never render as a review that found nothing. Name each spawn and its outcome: one of them going quiet is invisible here if only the other is described.

classes.description: One verdict per class, always present, so a class nobody reached is visible rather than absent.

findings.description: An empty items list under state checked is a review that ran and found nothing. Under state not-checked it is a review that never ran. Under state returned-nothing it is a review that ran, consumed its budget and handed back an empty final message, so its conclusions exist and are lost. Those are three different values and must never be spelled the same way.

disposition.description: What happened to the finding. There is deliberately no word here for a completed filing. `filed` used to be one, and it is past tense: read at the speed a maintainer reads a report -- states first, then items, most of them fixed -- it says this has been filed, while it meant this should be filed, by you, and nothing has happened yet. Twice in one day (#254) it meant nobody filed it, and both losses were invisible without leaving the report and searching the tracker, which is this repository's own defect class inside its own review contract. The value is removed rather than joined by a second one, because an agent must not file: the publishing clause is unconditional -- no push, no pull request, no comment on the issue -- and opening a tracker issue is publishing under the maintainer's credentials, in the one surface this plugin deliberately keeps agents out of. A vocabulary that lets an agent SAY filed makes a forbidden action spellable and, worse, spellable falsely. `report-for-filing` is the same word adjacent.action already uses for the same act: one vocabulary, present tense, and unmistakably a request addressed to somebody else. A report still carrying `filed` is refused rather than reinterpreted, and the contract number moved with it so an older copy reads as unvalidatable rather than as a malformed report. `below-bar` (#411) is the third receipt the filing bar defines and this enum could not spell: a real finding the agent judged below the intake bar, recorded in the pull request body instead. It applies here and not only to `adjacent` because a finding is below the bar or it is not, and who noticed it does not change that -- `refused` and `argued-down` are not substitutes, since both say the finding was WRONG and this one says it was right.

text.description: The finding as the reviewer put it, in full. One sentence is cheap; a boolean is unreadable.

reason.description: Required when the disposition is refused, argued-down, report-for-filing or below-bar: the argument, not a restatement. This is the field that keeps the orchestrator arguing with findings rather than scanning past them. `below-bar` needs it for the same reason `report-for-filing` does and a different one from `refused`: the maintainer is being asked NOT to open an issue, so what they need in order to leave it closed is why the agent judged the class unreachable.

pr_anchor.description: Required when the disposition is `below-bar`, and checked against the pull request body by the on-disk pass. Same field, same rules and same limits as $defs/adjacent/properties/pr_anchor -- one act, one vocabulary, whether the agent found the thing itself or a spawn handed it over.

pr_body.description: The agent writes the whole pull request -- title and body -- to a file the forge can consume unchanged, and names it here. The orchestrator reads it and hands it over. That deletes a translation step that costs a thousand tokens and loses detail on the way. Judgment does not move: the orchestrator still reads the body before it opens anything.

path.description: A .pr.json file holding the forge payload described by $defs/forge_payload -- NOT a markdown body. A markdown file is the shape a forge refuses, and the refusal lands on the orchestrator after the agent's session has ended, at which point somebody re-narrates the body and invents a title. The title is the sentence most people read and the only part that survives a squash into the log, so it belongs to whoever did the work. The payload must sit beside the report: the validator resolves this against the report's own directory and refuses -- without opening anything -- what lands outside it, because this value is written by an agent and the file it names is opened, parsed and quoted back by the maintainer's own process. An absolute path is fine and is what an agent in a worktree normally writes; what is checked is where it resolves to, not how it is spelled. Both sides are resolved, so a symlink sitting inside the report's directory and pointing out of it is refused too -- resolving reads link targets and opens nothing. That sentence was claimed in the function docstring and the changelog and asserted by nothing until #234, so a lexical normalisation would have kept every containment test green and made all three false at once. Deliberately no `pattern` here: containment depends on where the report itself is, which a regex cannot see, so a pattern could only be a second checker answering a narrower question -- and two checkers disagreeing about one input is its own defect. The whole check lives in one function and is named in x-enforced-on-disk.

closes.description: What merging this pull request will close, in three states, of which only the third is a defect: it closes something, it deliberately closes nothing, or nobody said. Required whenever state is `written`. Measured across two sessions, four of seven agent-written payloads bound no closing keyword to the issue they were written for; every one of them validated clean here because nothing looked at the body, and every one was caught at the maintainer's gh-pr-create call -- which REPORTS and does not refuse, exit 0 -- after the agent's session had ended. On the fourth the counterfactual was measured rather than argued: the manual repair was separable from the merge, and without it the merge would have closed nothing while the board read clean. Deliberately closing nothing is sayable the way gh-pr-edit's `unlink` token is sayable: a `Part of #N` pull request is a real decision and refusing it would be a gate inventing a rule. WHAT THE ON-DISK CHECK IS, said here so the weaker thing cannot be read as the stronger one: an ABSENCE detector, not a closing-reference reader. It reports that it could find no closing keyword bound to a declared number outside code spans and HTML comments; it never decides what a forge will close. Every transformation it makes can only make it report more often, so a finding is strong and a pass is weak. supertool publishes the one reader that does decide, and gh-pr, gh-pr-create and gh-pr-edit all use it; every route to it from here makes a forge call and two of them publish, so it is unreachable from a stdlib-only validator, and a second copy of a resolver is the drifting duplicate this repository forbids. On the two traps that make a substring grep wrong the detector is not merely conservative but correct: `Closes #A #B` closes only #A and #B is refused, and a backticked `Closes #A` closes nothing and is refused. Both shapes were observed in one night.

issues.description: Every issue number merging this closes. At least one is required when the state is `closes`, and each one is looked for in the payload's body with a closing keyword bound to it -- which is why a shared keyword over two numbers is refused for the second: that is what a forge does with it.

reason.description: Required when the state is `closes-nothing`. A deliberate re-scope and a forgotten keyword are one missing line apart, and without this they render identically.

forge_payload.description: The file at pr_body.path. JSON only, deliberately: a forge may also accept TOML, but TOML needs an interpreter-version-dependent parser and a check that cannot run on every supported interpreter would have to report a third state on some of them -- one shape, checkable everywhere, is worth more than the flexibility.

head.description: The branch the work is on. Checked against the report's own branch: the two disagreeing means a pull request opened from somewhere else, and the comparison is free once the file is open.

examples.head: 1dc856d
examples.summary: Suffix match now splits on either separator, so a Windows path stops being read as one long name. Red then green pasted below; one reviewer finding argued down.

files.change: split on either separator before matching a suffix
a backslash path and a POSIX path in the same fixture

red.note: the backslash case returned the whole path as the name

review.mechanism: general-purpose subagent pointed at the auditor brief in the plugin root

items.why: no input crosses a trust boundary in this diff
no benchmark exists in this repo to run

items.text: The assertion hardcodes a forward slash, so the new case passes on POSIX and cannot fail on Windows.
The helper should raise on an empty path rather than returning an empty string.
items.reason: Two callers already treat the empty string as absent and would start crashing on a case they handle today; raising is a behaviour change nobody filed.

items.why: the only sentence naming the helper describes what it returns, not how it splits; read it against the new behaviour and it is still true
held by the lane on #131 this run; the separator paragraph there almost certainly needs the same edit

items.text: The docstring above the helper still describes the single-separator behaviour.

examples.split_cost: Roughly two thirds to the note (the full reviewer exchange and the caller sweep); nothing was left out of both.
